t: Find the Array Concatenation Value — Two Pointers
o: Repeatedly concatenate the current first and last elements (adding the result to a running total) and remove them; if one element remains, add it alone. For [7,52,2,4]: 74 + 522 = 596. With n up to 1000 and values up to 1e4, any direct simulation works; the only care point is computing concatenation without string overhead if desired.
k: Concatenation of a and b equals a * 10^(digits of b) + b.
Two pointers from both ends naturally model the removal process.

a.n: Approach 1: Two pointers with arithmetic concatenation
a.i: Walk pointers l and r toward each other; at each step add cat(nums[l], nums[r]) computed as nums[l] * 10^digits(nums[r]) + nums[r]. When l == r add the lone element and stop.
s: While l < r: ans += cat(nums[l], nums[r]); l++, r--.
If l == r: ans += nums[l]. Return ans.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def findTheArrayConcVal(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        ans, l, r = 0, 0, len(nums) - 1
        while l < r:
            b = nums[r]
            p = 10
            while p <= b: p *= 10
            ans += nums[l] * p + b
            l += 1; r -= 1
        if l == r: ans += nums[l]
        return ans

a.t: O(n log M) — each element processed once; digit counting is O(log M) per pair.

a.i: Convert to strings and parse back — simplest to write and clearly correct, at slightly higher constant cost.
a.t: O(n log M) — same pointer walk with string conversions.

w: Either approach is fine given tiny constraints; prefer arithmetic concatenation to show fluency. Pitfalls: forgetting the odd-length middle element, and integer overflow in languages with fixed-width ints (use 64-bit: up to ~500 concatenations of 5-digit pairs fits comfortably). Follow-up: maximize/minimize the value by choosing pairing order instead.
